blocks.text: Here we must above all note the conception of the enormous size of the animal. While the largest species of crocodile, namely the Nile crocodile, reaches a length of at most 30 feet (Voigt l. c. 3, p. 31), the true whale is twice as long (60–61 feet; Voigt l. c. 1, p. 471 **). Furthermore, the obtaining of train oil can apply only to the whale, and finally the whale, whose flesh, when it is young, has the taste of pork, is more edible than the flesh of the crocodile, which has a musky odor and is therefore, though edible, nevertheless unpalatable. Also, the whalebone of the whale is thicker and longer than the ribs of the crocodile, so that the embellishment of our passage, which is in any case fabulously exaggerated, particularly regarding the making of the beams, still fits the whale far better than the crocodile.

This passage is followed by several others, in which fables are told about the enormous distance between the individual fins of the sea monster, but from which it at least emerges that it must be the whale, since, as mentioned, the crocodile has no fins. Admittedly, Raschbam (ibid.) errs in placing those fins on the [p. 158] back of the animal.
Finally, the said passage states expressly that the fish had two fins, which is indeed the case with the whale.
However, the Talmud also designated a fabulous animal by לויתן, about which we shall speak in detail in §. 505. Cf. also §. 347.

Conclusion. It is questionable which cetacean is meant in the Tosephot (Bechoroth 7b; s.v. רוב). It says here: One may eat the morays (מרנס, Muraenae) that are found in the רג בלי"נא. For מרנס the corresponding Piske Tosephot have הרינגן “herrings,” which do indeed form a main part of the whale's food; but Balaena is the generic name of various cetaceans; thus the cachalot is called Φάλαινα [phalaina] in Aristotle (Thierg. 1, 4, 1); yet it is more likely that the whale is meant in the Tosephot, since it has no teeth, which makes it possible for the herrings pressed down through the narrow gullet to remain whole and recognizable, whereas the cachalot (Cachelot) has pointed and somewhat curved teeth and therefore chews its food.

This cetacean, which is also called the sperm whale, is not, it is true, expressly named in the Talmud; yet, just as of the musk deer only the musk is mentioned (§. 150), so too of the cachalot only ambergris is mentioned, provided that the explanation of the Aruch were the more correct one among the divergent explanations, which, however, is highly questionable. Keritot 6a enumerates the species of which the incense in the Temple consisted. Among these a little of the כיפה הירדן was also taken, a species that is explained in various ways. Raschi considers it a kind of herb growing on the bank of the Jordan*); Aruch has two explanations, according to which that species is either a fragrant plant or ambergris.
